summary.text: Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime curvature, made by masses moving relative to one another, that spread outward at the speed of light.
They carry energy away as gravitational radiation, and because Newton's gravity acts instantly everywhere, his physics has no place for them.
Since they do not interact strongly with matter, they can show events and eras that light-based telescopes cannot reach.

facts.label: First direct detection
facts.value: September 2015, from two merging black holes

facts.label: First indirect evidence
facts.value: 1974, from a shrinking binary pulsar orbit

facts.label: Size on Earth
facts.value: Strains of less than 1 part in 10²⁰

facts.label: 2017 Nobel Prize
facts.value: Rainer Weiss, Kip Thorne and Barry Barish

facts.label: Planned space detector
facts.value: LISA, being developed by the European Space Agency

items.prompt: A friend says that if the Sun vanished, Earth would feel it the very same instant. What does that idea leave out that a wave would need?

options.label: Gravity being a much stronger force than it is
Gravity spreading outward at a limited speed
Gravity only acting on very heavy objects
Gravity changing the colour of nearby light

items.explain: Newton's law treats gravity as instant everywhere, so it has no wave that travels at a limited speed; waves appear only in general relativity.

items.prompt: Two astronauts float freely, far apart, when a gravitational wave passes through. What would a perfect measurement show?

options.label: The gap between them changes in step with the wave
Both are pushed the same way toward the source
Both are warmed by the energy of the wave
Nothing at all, since gravity pulls them equally

items.explain: A passing wave alters the separation of freely falling masses, and the change follows the waveform.

items.prompt: A wave source is moved to twice the distance from Earth. How does its effect on our instruments change?

options.label: It falls to a quarter of what it was
It stays the same, since waves never fade
It falls to half of what it was
It doubles because more space is crossed

items.explain: The effect is inversely proportional to distance, not distance squared, so doubling the distance halves it.

items.prompt: Cosmologists want to look at the universe before it became see-through to light. Why could gravitational waves help?

options.label: They are brighter than any light source
They travel much faster than light does
They are produced only by stars like ours
They hardly interact with matter in the way light does

items.explain: Before recombination the universe was opaque to light, but gravitational waves do not strongly interact with matter, so they offer a way to look that far back.

items.prompt: Astronomers watch two neutron stars circle each other and see the orbit shrink just as relativity says it should if energy leaks away as waves. How should this be described?

options.label: A direct detection by laser instruments
Indirect evidence that the waves exist
A failure of general relativity
A measurement of waves from a supernova

items.explain: The orbital decay of the Hulse-Taylor pulsar in 1974 matched the prediction for energy lost to gravitational radiation, which was the first indirect evidence.

items.prompt: In 2015 a first direct signal was caught. What event produced it?

options.label: A comet passing close to the Sun
A massive star fading out quietly
The merging of two black holes
Two galaxies passing through each other

items.explain: The first direct observation came from a signal generated by the merger of two black holes, received at LIGO's two sites.
